  • What determines your baby’s hair colour?
Pregnancy

What determines your baby’s hair colour?

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

It is natural to wonder whether your baby will have your hair, your partner’s eyes or a familiar grandparent’s features. That curiosity sometimes comes with advice about foods or habits said to change a baby’s appearance. Hair colour is strongly influenced by inherited biology. There is no proven pregnancy diet or home remedy that lets you choose blond hair, and no colour is a sign of better health.

Genes, chromosomes and family resemblance

Genes are stretches of DNA that contain biological instructions. Much of that DNA is packaged into chromosomes. A baby typically receives 23 chromosomes from the egg and 23 from the sperm, making 46 in total. The combination brings together inherited information from both sides of the family.

Different versions of a gene are called alleles. For many genes, a person has two copies, one inherited from each biological parent. The versions passed on are not necessarily obvious from a parent’s appearance. That helps explain why a baby may resemble one parent in some ways and other relatives in others.

Chromosomes are not a simple catalogue in which every visible feature has a single switch. Many characteristics involve several genes and the way they function during development. Family resemblance gives clues, but it cannot provide a precise preview of a baby’s face, skin, eyes or hair.

What gives hair its colour?

Hair colour depends on pigments called melanins. Eumelanin contributes brown and black colouring; small amounts are associated with blond shades. Pheomelanin contributes red tones. The balance and amount of these pigments produce a broad range of natural colours.

Many genes affect pigment production and related processes. This is why hair comes in more shades than a simple brown-versus-blond choice. Two people described as having brown hair may carry different combinations of pigment-related variants.

The science is well established that genes and pigment matter, even though researchers are still investigating all the contributions and interactions. Uncertainty about an individual prediction does not mean that hair colour is simply guesswork or that a food remedy can override it.

Why the dominant-brown, recessive-blond rule is incomplete

Introductory explanations sometimes imagine one gene with a brown version and a blond version. In that model, a brown version masks a blond version, while two blond versions produce blond hair. It can illustrate how an inherited feature may be less visible in one generation.

Real hair colour is more complex. Several genes contribute, so the model should not be used as a complete rule for your child. It does not justify saying that one brown allele always guarantees brown hair or that every blond child must have one particular pair of blond alleles.

Two dark-haired parents can have a lighter-haired child because their visible hair does not reveal all their inherited variants. The absence of a known blond relative is not proof that blond hair is impossible. Likewise, family photographs and online colour charts cannot establish biological parentage.

What is established at conception, and what can change later?

The inherited genetic combination is established when the egg and sperm join. Changing what you eat after that does not replace the variants your baby inherited. In that sense, the basis for inherited appearance is present from the beginning of pregnancy.

However, this does not mean that the exact visible hair shade is fixed forever at conception or at birth. Pigment production can change as a child grows, and some children’s light hair becomes darker. A baby’s early appearance is therefore not a guaranteed forecast of their teenage or adult hair colour.

If your child eventually has a different shade from the one you first noticed, that does not show that a pregnancy food or habit succeeded or failed. Development and inherited variation provide a more useful explanation than looking back for something you ate.

Can yogurt, seawater or avoiding sunlight make a baby blond?

There is no evidence-based food, drink or sunlight-avoidance routine that can make an unborn baby blond. Yogurt can be part of a suitable pregnancy diet, but its colour and nutrients do not select a baby’s hair pigment. You do not need to eat extra amounts for this purpose.

Do not drink seawater to try to change your baby’s appearance. Its salt content can be dangerous and worsen dehydration. Products or folk preparations promoted under names such as “sea foam” are also not a validated way to change inherited hair colour; their identity and safety should never be assumed from the name.

Avoiding daylight does not choose a baby’s hair colour either. Decisions about sun protection and any recommended supplements should be based on your own health needs. A claim about a more desirable-looking baby is not a sound reason to alter those habits or take an unreviewed preparation.

Where pregnancy care can make a difference

Eating a varied diet supports your health and your baby’s growth. Follow appropriate food-safety advice, use the supplements recommended for your circumstances and attend antenatal appointments. These practical steps have a different purpose from trying to select a cosmetic trait.

You do not need a special menu for a blond baby. If someone recommends a powder, herb or high-dose supplement for appearance, show the product to a pharmacist or your maternity clinician before using it. A natural label does not establish that it is suitable in pregnancy.

Enjoy imagining family resemblances without turning them into a test of your pregnancy choices. Your child may look familiar in unexpected ways, and their appearance may change with time. Hair colour is not a measure of how well you cared for them.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Hair colour is influenced by many genes and the amount and type of melanin.

Simple dominant/recessive examples cannot reliably predict an individual child’s shade.

Inherited variants are present from conception, while visible hair colour may change during childhood.

Use food and supplements to support health, not to try to choose a baby’s appearance.

How BeMama can help

Keep appearance predictions light-hearted. If advice involves swallowing a substance or changing your diet, ask what evidence supports it and whether it is safe in pregnancy. Save questions about products for your next maternity or pharmacy conversation.

When to seek help

Do not drink seawater or take an unknown preparation to influence a baby’s appearance. If you have swallowed something potentially harmful, contact a local poison-information service or clinician promptly; seek emergency care if seriously unwell.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • No pregnancy food or home remedy can reliably make a baby blond.
  • Hair colour involves many inherited variants, not one simple colour switch.
  • A child’s hair may differ from both parents’ visible shades.
  • Hair colour can change as a child grows.
  • Choose pregnancy nutrition for health, not a promised appearance.

Frequently asked questions

How is a baby’s hair colour determined?

Inherited variants affect the pigments made in hair. Many genes contribute, which makes real inheritance more complex than a single brown-or-blond rule.

Is hair colour decided at conception?

The inherited genetic combination is established then, but the visible shade can change as pigment production changes with growth. Birth hair is not necessarily the lifelong colour.

Can two brown-haired parents have a blond child?

Yes. Visible hair colour does not show every inherited variant, and several genes are involved. A family tree alone cannot give certainty.

Will eating yogurt make my baby blond?

No. Yogurt may fit into your pregnancy diet, but it does not select your baby’s hair colour. There is no need to eat extra for that purpose.

Does drinking seawater help?

No. It does not change inherited hair colour and can be dangerous because of its salt content. Do not use it as a pregnancy remedy.

Can avoiding the sun change my unborn baby’s hair?

There is no validated sunlight-avoidance routine for selecting fetal hair colour. Follow ordinary health and sun-protection advice.

Is there any safe home method for choosing a baby’s hair colour?

No proven food, supplement or household method does that. Focus on appropriate antenatal care and a varied diet instead.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
